Good morning. Distinguished delegates, participants and representatives of indigenous peoples, I have the honor to welcome you to this session. And before we begin with agenda item nine this morning on enhanced participation, I have the distinct pleasure to welcome the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, His Excellency Volker Turk. While he was unable to join us for the opening session on Monday morning, we are particularly pleased to welcome him and have him here with us today. So, High Commissioner, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam Chair, distinguished members of the expert mechanism, Representatives of indigenous peoples, excellencies, colleagues and friends, real pleasure to be here and I honor the presence of indigenous peoples from every region of the world at this session of the expert mechanism on the rights of indigenous people. Your participation has been key to the creation and achievement of this body. More broadly, your contributions have led and nourished our efforts to advance the rights of indigenous peoples to self-determination, to participation, to non-discrimination, to justice and more. At a time of profound global uncertainty, indigenous peoples continue to demonstrate leadership and leadership that the world urgently needs. Your knowledge systems contribute directly to biodiversity conservation, to climate resilience, to sustainable resource management and to social cohesion. Across the world indigenous young people are spearheading work to address climate change, to protect biodiversity, to revitalize languages, to preserve cultural heritage and to promote human rights. Indigenous peoples' rights are not theoretical aspirations for the future, they are obligations for the present, now. And wherever those rights are respected, all of society becomes more just, more peaceful, and more resilient. Yet, a persistent gap remains between international commitments to indigenous peoples' rights and their implementation in practice. Mining and extractive activities, deforestation, and large-scale agriculture exploit and destroy lands and territories without the consent of indigenous peoples. These concerns are becoming more urgent. Growing demand for critical minerals, renewable energy infrastructure, and large-scale development projects is placing increasing pressure on indigenous lands and territories. The world's transition to a greener economy is essential but it cannot come at the expense of the rights of indigenous peoples. There needs to be a just transition firmly grounded in human rights, meaningful participation and consent to all projects affecting their territories and resources. Indigenous environmental human rights defenders, including many women and young people, face widespread intimidation, criminalization, harassment and violence for defending their lands and ecosystems. Between 2023 and 2025, at least 15% of the human rights defenders killed or forcibly disappeared around the world were indigenous human rights defenders. I want to emphasize this disproportionate and unacceptable impact on indigenous activists. In addition, indigenous peoples are often targeted for prosecution and their legitimate activities criminalized based on broad and vaguely worded laws on terrorism and extremism. The death of the Nicaraguan Misquito leader Brooklyn Rivera six weeks ago while arbitrarily detained reflects such patterns of repression. In this era of turmoil, conflict is surging across many regions. Indigenous peoples are among those facing loss, displacement and the misery that it engenders. This year's study by the expert mechanism on the rights of indigenous peoples in conflict and post-conflict situations sheds light on these issues and makes clear that systemic issues need to be resolved if peace is to be achieved. Historical injustices, dispossession of lands and resources, denial of self-determination, systematic discrimination and inequalities, environmental degradation, and the erosion of their governance systems are some of the factors that shape the violence inflicted on indigenous peoples. Yet indigenous peoples have played a long-standing and central role in building peace through governance systems and customary law that support accountability and restoration, and traditional practices that are conducive to social harmony. Examples include the efforts of the Mazahua, Otomi, Nahua, Matlatzinca, and Tlahuica peoples in Mexico, for example. Duro peace requires inclusion, justice, meaningful participation at every stage, and recognition of rights. and this must involve recognition of indigenous people's rights to self-determination and to control over their lands. In this context, the work of this expert mechanism is key to bringing international standards to life in practice. I welcome your recent engagement in Brazil to examine the protection of indigenous peoples who choose to remain in voluntary isolation or who have come into initial contact with the majority population. This engagement demonstrated the value of dialogue among indigenous peoples, governments and human rights mechanisms in relation to land rights, environmental degradation, illegal mining and violence. These lessons resonate far beyond one country. I also welcome recent advances in domestic courts In May, an indigenous group in Australia secured record compensation for mining conducted without their consent, a significant step towards accountability and redress. Distinguished participants, humanity's oldest tradition can and must help us to guide our newest innovations. The expert mechanism has produced far-sighted and useful work on artificial intelligence and digital systems. Data is a cultural, strategic, and economic resource that can be misused to fuel discrimination and dispossession. Indigenous peoples need to be able to exercise control over data relating to their communities and knowledge systems, and I look forward to the expert mechanisms further examination of these issues at this session. I also urge states to strengthen their support for the UN Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples, which has enabled thousands of representatives of indigenous peoples to bring their voices to international forum. And finally, but importantly, I encourage all of you to join our Global Alliance for Human Rights, which we launched last month. It will link the work of doers and thinkers from every region, sector and age group, pooling the thoughts of people working from the Amazon to the Arctic into a great river of solutions for human rights, and I invite indigenous peoples to participate. Together we can work to place all human rights at the center of decision making everywhere. Thank you very much.

I would like to thank the High Commissioner with most gratitude for the statement today and for joining us every year. We appreciate so deeply the High Commissioner's commitment to the advancement of the rights of indigenous peoples and to human rights more generally. And I would just like to express a personal note of gratitude. This will be my last time sharing the podium with you as a member of the expert mechanism. And I just want to express my deepest thanks for your work in the area of human rights. And I look forward to working with you in my academic capacity in future.
Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you.

Okay. Item nine, enhancing the participation of indigenous peoples in the United Nations. So on behalf of the expert mechanism, I once again want to welcome all participants to the room, indigenous peoples, member states, NGOs, and all others. It's my pleasure to preside over this discussion on enhancing the participation of indigenous peoples in the United Nations. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples explicitly addresses the role of the United Nations in the full realization of its provisions in Article 41. The declaration goes as far as stating the ways and means of ensuring participation of indigenous peoples on issues affecting them shall be established. In resolutions 5412 of 2023 and 5715 of 2024, the Human Rights Council decided to continue discussions and develop further steps and measures necessary to enable and facilitate the participation of indigenous peoples representatives and institutions in its work. Following the previous work on concrete ways to enhance the participation of indigenous peoples in the work of the Human Rights Council, including through the July and October 2024 intercessional meetings, and the October 2025 Human Rights Council resolution on indigenous peoples, the expert mechanism wants to consider what the best strategic next steps on this work would be. We posted guiding questions to facilitate today's dialogue. We look forward to hearing your suggestions and recommendations on enhancing participation of indigenous peoples in the United Nations. including specifically on questions of what concrete steps can be taken to establish a clear roadmap and timeline to enhance the participation of indigenous peoples in the work of the Human Rights Council. What measures are required to effectively implement the recommendations contained in the joint report of the co-facilitators and the OHCHR? and what immediate steps can be taken to accelerate progress in enhancing participation ahead of the forthcoming sessions of the Human Rights Council. The expert mechanism would like to continue on the momentum of this important work and facilitate broad discussions between indigenous peoples, member states, and other key stakeholders in the room today, starting with the panel, Starting to address the following issues. To continue contributing to the discussion on the ongoing process of enhancing indigenous participation in the United Nations. and based on the desire of indigenous peoples for clarity on the roadmap and timeline going forward and to identify concrete recommendations to accelerate efforts. It's the strong view of the EMRIP that it is absolutely essential that an indigenous led mechanism be established to accredit indigenous peoples. The expert mechanism feels that it could potentially play a role for the accreditation, although there are Concerns about the resources necessary to do this work and how the secretariat could be better supported, both technically and budgetarily in its administrative capacity. It must be reiterated that the expert mechanism's priority is our mandate to interpret, clarify, and provide advice on the implementation of the UN declaration. We strongly recognize and respect indigenous people's stated desire for an independent accreditation mechanism and we support the future development of such an entity. I'd now like to turn to the speakers list. Actually, before we move to the speakers list, the EMRIP would like to offer a couple of reminders to the room. And before we proceed, we need to recall that the United Nations promotes dialogue and exchanges between different actors with a view to promoting sustainable peace, development, and human rights. All participants are encouraged to contribute to EMRIP in a spirit of constructive, multi-stakeholder dialogue, keeping a focus on the theme of the discussion. And the meetings of the expert mechanism, as any UN system events, are guided by the highest ethical and professional standards. And all participants are expected to behave with integrity and respect towards other participants attending or involved with any meeting of the EMRIP. We count on your cooperation to ensure that these standards are adhered to by all participants in this session. We ask all participants to exercise decorum, avoid abusive or disrespectful language or any derogatory or inflammatory remarks. As established in the UN code of conduct to prevent harassment at UN events, the UN system is committed to enabling events where everyone can participate in an inclusive, respectful and safe environment. And this includes without fear of intimidation or reprisals of any sort. The Human Rights Council resolution 3325 of 2016 established that the expert mechanism shall determine its own methods of work, although the expert mechanism may not adopt resolutions or decisions. The same resolution established that the annual meeting of the expert mechanism shall be open to the participation as observers of states, UN mechanisms, bodies and specialized agencies, funds and programs, intergovernmental organizations, regional organizations and mechanisms in the field of human rights, national human rights institutions and other relevant national bodies, academics, experts and non-governmental organizations. With those reminders, we will proceed with the speakers list. I would first like to call Asia Indigenous Peoples Caucus. You have the floor.

With the support of the UN Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples, I participated in both intercessional meetings on enhanced participation on Indigenous Peoples and the work on the Human Rights Council. Having been part of this process, we welcome the progress made so far. However, from the perspective of indigenous peoples in Asia, we stress that the time has come to move from the repeated discussions to concrete implementation. The Human Rights Council must establish a clear roadmap, timeline and responsibility for the implementation. Participation must recognize indigenous peoples not merely as NGOs or civil society, but the peoples with the rights to self-determination reflecting our status and representative institutions. In Asia, many indigenous peoples are still not recognized as indigenous by the states. The absence of states recognition does not mean that we do not exist as peoples. Accreditation must therefore be independent, transparent and indigenous threat. States must not have veto power over who represent us. Protection against the must also been integral parts of enhanced participation. Across Asia, indigenous peoples are representatives and human rights defenders face savagery and intimidation, criminalization and militarization for defending our lands, territories and resources and rights. Some are even targeted as terrorists or treated as threats to national security. If we can speak on the UN, but face threats or criminalization when we return home, this is not safe or meaningful participation. Meaningful participation is also more than a short statement in a meeting. Indigenous peoples' political institutions and representative organization must have meaningful input into consultation, negotiation, legislation, reports, and then other council outcome. Adequate funding, interpretation, visa support, accessibility, and timely access to information must be also ensured.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm speaking for the Coalition for the Human Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and I'll try to be brief. Thank you very much for your statement. Appreciate that. I would next like to offer the floor to Australia.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Australia reaffirms its longstanding position that meaningful Indigenous participation is fundamental to the fairness and integrity of human rights and United Nations processes. Australia was proud to be a state co-facilitator, alongside Canada, of the intercessional meetings of the Human Rights Council in 2024 and its subsequent joint report. These meetings progressed the 2023 decision to establish a distinct status for Indigenous peoples accreditation at select HRC meetings. Australia would like to reiterate key recommendations for the accreditation process from the intersessional meetings. The process must be rooted in the principles of UNDRIP, including self-determination, self-identification, flexibility, equality among Indigenous socio-cultural regions, non-discrimination, transparency, and accountability. Accreditation should be guided in a flexible manner, including through the elements outlined in the joint report. Notably, it should be chosen by indigenous peoples in accordance with their own procedures and be legitimately representative of their peoples. Australia encourages the HRC to take forward these recommendations. Recent advances in the HRC also serve as a positive example for the rest of the UN system, including the work of the President of the General Assembly. Australia encourages innovative ideas by which indigenous peoples' right to participation can be further enhanced in line with UN reform objectives. Australia also encourages member states to support the UN Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples. The voluntary fund helps to overcome one of the key obstacles to indigenous peoples' attendance at UN meetings, the financial costs. Chair, as participation is enhanced, there is also a real risk that exposure to reprisals may increase as well. All forms of reprisals must be condemned unequivocally and addressed promptly to ensure indigenous peoples can participate freely, safely, and fully in discussions on issues that impact them. Thank you.
Thank you very much for your statement. I'd next like to give the floor to United Confederation of Taino People.

Abundant blessings, Chair, distinguished experts, and indigenous relatives. My name is Dr. Lisette Rivera Guane, and I am a 2026 UN Indigenous Fellow. Despite centuries of colonization, Taino peoples continue to live, organize, and revitalize our culture and exercise our inherent rights throughout the Caribbean and the diaspora. UNDRIP affirms in articles 3, 5, 18, and 33 our right to self-determination, to maintain our institutions, to participate in decision-making, and to determine our own identity and membership. Yet indigenous peoples living in non-self-governing, unincorporated, and other territories that remain under colonial administration continue to face barriers to the full realization of these rights. More than 112,000 individuals identified as Taiyo in the 2020 United States Census, including 30,000 people in Borinquen, Puerto Rico. Despite this documented presence, our peoples often remain overlooked in indigenous policy discussions and insufficiently represented in decisions affecting our communities and futures. There are many indigenous peoples globally living under territorial and colonial status whose circumstances remain insufficiently examined within the UN systems. This gap limits meaningful participation and hinders implementation of the declaration. consistent with articles 41 and 42 which call upon UN bodies and mechanisms to contribute to the realization and implementation of indigenous people's rights we recommend that EMRIP conduct a study on the implementation of UNDRIP in non-self-governing unincorporated and other territories that remain under colonial administration without greater understanding of these distinct territorial contexts efforts to enhance indigenous people's participation within the United Nations system will remain incomplete the UCTP is ready to collaborate.
Thank you very much for your statement. I'd next like to offer the floor to Inuit Circumpolar Council.

Madam Chair, Inuit Circumpolar Council wishes to reiterate our support for the Indigenous Coordinating Body and call for member states to support ICB and the enhanced participation process through funding and hosting of events and gatherings related to this process. And as I'm taking the floor for the last time at this session, I would like to congratulate the chair, election of the chair and the vice chairs for the EMRIP and look forward to continue the cooperation in the future.

Madam Chair, The National Iwi Chairs Forum welcomes the discussion and supports the proposals advanced yesterday by the Indigenous Coordinating Body, the Indigenous Determinants of Health Alliance, and the International Indian Treaty Council. Thank you, Madam Chair. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of Australia, Denmark, Finland, Guatemala, Mexico, Norway, and my own country, Canada. We thank the Chair, the expert members and the Office of the High Commissioner for their continued work to advance discussions on enhancing the participation of indigenous peoples at the Human Rights Council and United Nations more broadly. We also recognize the engagement and active contributions of Member States to advance in a measured but concrete manner towards this goal. Over the last few years, we have made significant progress and we believe we should continue moving forward. The recommendations contained in the joint report 5935 of the co-facilitators and the OHCHR on ways to enhance participation provide a strong foundation for action. Their implementation would advance the effective realization of the UNDRIP whose 20th anniversary should serve as a further impetus to move beyond discussions. The Council should consider establishing a clear roadmap with defined milestones and timelines to follow up on the accreditation principles contained in the joint report, as decided in HRC resolution 60/13. This process should include regular consultations with indigenous peoples and periodic reporting on progress. We welcome a constructive and forward-looking approach taking into account financial constraints. Member States should further prioritize discussions on how to reduce procedural and structural barriers that limit access and participation. In doing so, efforts should make effective use of existing resources and mechanisms with financial and technical support, interpretation services, and opportunities for remote participation. Meaningful participation requires that indigenous peoples have opportunities not only to speak, but also to shape outcomes. We particularly look forward to the next interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur, the expert mechanism, as well as the annual panel discussion on the rights of indigenous peoples at the next council session. Thank you, Madam Chair. UNDRIP places participation at the heart of the protection and promotion of indigenous peoples. Article 41 affirms the responsibility of the United Nations system to ensure the participation of indigenous peoples in matters affecting them. This commitment is reinforced throughout the declaration. Article 5 recognizes the rights of indigenous peoples to participate fully in the political, economic, social and cultural life of the state in which they reside. Article 18 guarantees indigenous peoples' rights to participation in decision-making in matters affecting their rights. Article 27 further requires indigenous peoples' participation in processes concerning the recognition and protection of their lands, territories and resources. These provisions demonstrate the importance of the rights to participation for indigenous peoples. As the body interested to assist member states in achieving the goals of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People, EMRIP should actively promote a meaningful, effective, informed, inclusive, and non-discriminatory participation of all indigenous peoples across all the seven UN socio-cultural regions in the UN system, including within our mechanism. Contemporary human rights, jurisprudence and scholarship recognizes participation not merely as a procedural mechanism for realizing other rights, but also as an autonomous substantive right in itself. Meaningful participation therefore requires more than symbolic representation, as mentioned by many in the room, but it also demands the genuine inclusion and equitable participation of indigenous peoples in decision making, including leadership level. As EMRIP, we can advance this objective by strengthening and consistently applying the established practice of rotational leadership. A transparent, inclusive and predictable rotation of leadership would provide each socio-cultural region with a fair opportunity to serve, reflecting the principle of equality, non-discrimination, and self-determination that underpins the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People. Such an approach would not only enhance the legitimacy and credibility of the mechanism and the UN system at large, but also fosters trust, shared ownership, and unity among indigenous representatives. At a time when the rights of indigenous peoples face increasing challenge across the globe, our collective priority must be to strengthen unity, mutual respect, inclusivity, and meaningful participation of all indigenous peoples from across the seven UN social cultural regions in the UN system. I thank you, Madam Chair.
